points.title: Three specialised OS types
points.must: Real-time, network and batch processing OS, each with its main goal (deadline / shared network resources / large volumes of similar jobs) and an example of where it is used.
points.model: Real-time OS — responds within a guaranteed deadline (embedded/control systems, e.g. ABS). Network OS — manages shared network resources and users (school/office servers, e.g. Windows Server). Batch OS — processes large volumes of similar jobs without interaction (banks, utility bills).

points.title: Definition of an RTOS
points.must: An OS that processes data and responds to events within a strict, guaranteed time limit (deadline) to monitor and control a physical process as it happens.
points.model: RTOS — an operating system that processes data and responds to events within a strict, guaranteed time limit (deadline), so it can monitor and control a physical process as it happens. 'Real-time' = on time, not just fast; a late result is a wrong result.

points.title: RTOS feedback loop
points.must: Sensor → RTOS decides within the deadline → actuator → physical process → sensor again, with an example such as a greenhouse or airbag.
points.model: Sensor (input) → RTOS / control program compares with the set value within the deadline → actuator (output: motor, valve, heater) → physical process changes → sensor measures again. Greenhouse: 32 °C > 30 °C → windows open within 2 s. Airbag must inflate within ~30 ms.

points.title: Features of an RTOS
points.must: At least four: deterministic response, priority-based pre-emptive scheduling, fast interrupt handling / low latency, continuous monitoring, reliability / fault tolerance, small and embedded.
points.model: Deterministic (predictable, bounded response time); priority-based pre-emptive scheduling; fast interrupt handling / low interrupt latency; continuous monitoring with feedback; high reliability / fault tolerance, runs for years; small and efficient, embedded in ROM/flash, little or no user interface.

points.title: Interrupts and pre-emption
points.must: An interrupt is a signal that an event needs attention now; tasks have priorities; the highest-priority task pre-empts a lower-priority task and finishes before its deadline; interrupt latency is short and bounded.
points.model: Interrupt — a signal from hardware/software that an event needs attention now. Tasks have priorities; the RTOS saves the running task, pre-empts it and runs the more urgent task, then resumes the interrupted task. Interrupt latency = time from interrupt to start of the handling task; kept short and bounded.

points.title: Hard and soft real-time
points.must: Hard: a missed deadline is a failure and may be dangerous (airbag, ABS, pacemaker); soft: a missed deadline only lowers quality (video call, online game).
points.model: Hard real-time — a missed deadline is a system failure, may be dangerous: airbag, ABS, pacemaker, flight control. Soft real-time — a missed deadline only lowers quality, the system keeps working: video call, streaming, online game.

points.title: RTOS vs general-purpose OS
points.must: RTOS meets every deadline with deterministic response and minimal interface; a general-purpose OS aims for good average speed, time-sharing and a rich GUI.
points.model: RTOS: meets every deadline, strict priority pre-emptive scheduling, deterministic response, small, minimal interface. General-purpose OS (Windows): good average speed, fair time-sharing between programs, response varies with load (background updates), large, rich GUI.

points.title: Definition of a NOS
points.must: An OS, usually on a server, that manages a network: its shared resources (files, printers, applications, Internet access) and the users who access them.
points.model: Network operating system — an OS, usually on a server, that manages a network: its shared resources (files, printers, applications, Internet access) and the users who access them; client computers connect to it (client–server).

points.title: Functions of a NOS
points.must: At least five: user accounts and groups, authentication, authorisation / access rights, file and printer sharing, security and audit logs, central backup and updates, remote administration.
points.model: User account and group management, password policies; authentication; authorisation / access rights; file and printer sharing (print queues, home folders); security (firewall, audit logs); centralised backup and software updates; remote administration, DHCP/DNS/e-mail; many users at once.

points.title: User account management
points.must: Accounts in groups → log-in → authentication (who are you?) → authorisation (what may you access?) → access only to allowed resources, logged; with an access-rights example.
points.model: Admin creates accounts and puts them in groups (Teachers, Grade 12); rights are given to groups. Log-in: authentication = who are you? (user name + password, 2FA); authorisation = what may you access? (rights of account and groups). Example: \\Exams teachers read/write, pupils no access; access is logged; leaver's account disabled in one place.

points.title: Client–server vs peer-to-peer
points.must: Client–server: central control, stronger security, central backup, needs a server and administrator, for large networks; peer-to-peer: each computer manages itself, cheap, for small networks.
points.model: Client–server (NOS on a server): centralised control, strong security set in one place, central automatic backup, needs a server and administrator, server is a single point of failure, for large networks. Peer-to-peer: each computer manages itself, weaker security, users back up themselves, cheap and simple, for home/small office.

points.title: Definition of a batch processing OS
points.must: Groups jobs with similar requirements and runs them one after another automatically, without user interaction, usually at a scheduled time; data is collected over a period and processed together.
points.model: Batch processing OS — groups jobs with similar requirements into batches and runs them one after another automatically, without user interaction, usually at a scheduled (off-peak) time; data is collected over a period and processed together.

points.title: How batch processing works
points.must: Collect data in a transaction file → sort to match the master file → submit jobs with JCL / script to a job queue → run at night with no operator, matching each transaction to its master record → new master file, output spooled; definition of spooling.
points.model: Data collected in a transaction file → sorted into the order of the master file (key field) → jobs submitted with JCL/script to a job queue → run at night with no operator, one sequential pass matching transactions to master records → new master file; output spooled. Spooling — output for a slow device queued on disk so the processor continues with the next job.

points.title: Uses, advantages and disadvantages of batch
points.must: Uses (payroll, bills, bank statements, card payments); advantages (efficient for large volumes, off-peak, no operator); disadvantages (delay, errors found late, no interaction).
points.model: Uses: payroll, utility bills, bank statements, end-of-day card payments, exam results, backups. Advantages: efficient for large volumes of similar data, uses off-peak time, no operator, consistent. Disadvantages: delay (results not immediate), errors found only after the batch, jobs cannot be changed while running, not for interactive/urgent tasks.

points.title: Choosing an OS type
points.must: For a scenario, name the OS type and give a reason linked to the scenario (e.g. ABS → hard real-time; school files → NOS; water bills → batch).
points.model: Ask: late response = failure? → real-time (dangerous → hard). Many users sharing resources with central security? → NOS. Large volume of similar data that can wait? → batch. Give a reason linked to the scenario: ABS → hard real-time; school of 900 pupils → NOS; 300 000 water bills → batch; video call → soft real-time.
